tier_reason: The first-party blog post by dchigarev, Modin's #3 contributor, states 'you get a 7x speed-up for this groupby' against pandas on a named Xeon W-2245, and gives Modin 0.28.0, pandas 2.2.1, Ray 2.9.1 and Python 3.9.18. The scripts are public (dchigarev/modin_perf_examples gh_page_1/customer_segmentation_simplified.py, which has a PANDAS_MODE=Pandas/Modin/Mixed switch). The 7x is a rounded figure, the dataset size is not stated on the page, and no compiler or flags are given, so it stays C.

corrections.workload: Kaggle 'customer-segmentation' workflow (its data.csv; size not stated on the page) run in a mixed mode where only the heavy groupby().apply() with a custom aggregation is wrapped in Modin. The page also has a 'heaviest pandas operations' showcase chart and a for-loop anti-pattern example; the linked for_loop_vs_groupby.py script uses 10M rows x 10 columns with 1M unique goods (about 80 s loop).
corrections.caveats: The blog is by Dmitry Chigarev (dchigarev), the #3 contributor to modin-project/modin, so it is first-party, not independent. Contrary to the earlier caveat, the appendix does state the hardware (HP ZCentral 4R, Xeon W-2245 8C/16T, 64 GB), Modin 0.28.0, pandas 2.2.1, Ray 2.9.1, Python 3.9.18 and Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, and the scripts are public in dchigarev/modin_perf_examples. The 7x is a rounded text figure and the groupby dataset size is not stated on the page. The author says Modin tends to win only when a pandas op takes more than 5 s, that full-Modin adoption slowed other parts of the workflow, and that the for-loop example is an anti-pattern where Modin should not be used.

notes: The record's claim matches the page. I corrected the caveat that said versions were missing (they are in the appendix) and noted that the benchmark scripts are public. It is near-A apart from the missing compiler/flags and dataset size, so it stays C.

tier_reason: The 1059x/1922x/10833x and 4.5x-31x (Q#2 81.4 vs 6.5 GB/s) figures do appear on the announcement, but they are for the closed TensorBase Frontier Edition 2021.3.0.a JIT engine, not the Apache-2.0 code in this repo. The repo's own docs/benchmarks.md (the same table as tensorbase/benchmarks quick.md) is first-party, names the CPU (Xeon Platinum 8260) and ClickHouse v21.2.5.5, and gives SQL queries but no scripts, compiler or flags, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Open-source main branch (repo docs/benchmarks.md, also tensorbase/benchmarks quick.md) vs ClickHouse v21.2.5.5 on the 1.46B-row NYC Taxi trips_lite table, in memory, best of 3: 3.1x faster on select sum(trip_id) (0.079 s vs 0.248 s), but 0.15x, i.e. about 6.7x slower, on a year group-by count (3.375 s vs 0.514 s). The README also claims 2x faster write throughput. The 1059x-10833x synthetic system.numbers ratios and the 4.5x-31.4x NYC Taxi ratios (Q#2 81.4 vs 6.52 GB/s) in the 2021-03-16 announcement belong to the closed TensorBase Frontier Edition 2021.3.0.a, which is not in this repo.
corrections.workload: NYC Taxi trips_lite (1,464,781,690 rows, two columns trip_id and pickup_datetime), in-memory single-table queries: sum(trip_id) and a year group-by count, vs ClickHouse v21.2.5.5. The FE announcement also had synthetic system.numbers aggregations and five NYC Taxi queries (Q#1-Q#5).
corrections.hardware: 1 socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8260, 24 cores / 48 hyperthreads, 6-channel DDR4-2400 ECC REG, 192 GB (repo docs/benchmarks.md; the FE README gives the same machine)
corrections.caveats: All numbers are first-party. The headline announcement figures come from the closed-source Frontier Edition JIT engine (the tensorbase_frontier_edition repo has no license, 9 stars, README and data only; the README says the JIT engine is 'not completely open sourced'). The synthetic 1000x-10000x ratios come from constant-folding the system.numbers loop, and the FE README itself says they 'make no senses for the real world'. For the open-source code the result is mixed: 3.1x faster on a simple sum and about 6.7x slower on a group-by. No compiler or flags are stated. The last commit was May 2022 and the README says no new features are planned, so the project is abandoned.

notes: The claim as recorded is overstated for this repo because it quotes a separate closed edition's numbers. I re-pointed it to the repo's own mixed benchmark (3.1x faster sum, 6.7x slower group-by). Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 1,462 stars, last commit 2022-05-10, not archived.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The companion paper was peer-reviewed and published at ICDE 2024, Industrial and Application Track (DOI 10.1109/ICDE60146.2024.00392, pp. 5211-5223, per Crossref). It shows wins over pandas, Dask, Modin and PySpark with stated versions on AWS r6i instances, and TPC-H code is in the repo (benchmarks/tpch/run_queries.py). The paper names no CPU model, compiler or flags, so it cannot reach A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Docs comparisons page: on TPC-H SF100, '~8 times faster than DaskDF and ~4 times quicker than Modin', with Koalas 'comparable' in speed but hitting task failures; at SF1000 Xorbits ran all queries while DaskDF, Koalas and Modin 'stumbled on most'. ICDE 2024 paper: 2.66x average speedup over the fastest baseline on operations all baselines support; 29x faster than Dask and 37x faster than Modin on TPCx-AI UC10 SF100 (data skew); 2.65x faster than Modin (the fastest baseline) on the census pipeline; 3.86x faster than PySpark on plasticc; pandas was slowest on the single-node pipelines (figure only, no ratio given).
corrections.hardware: Paper: AWS r6i family; supervisor on r6i.large, workers on up to 16 r6i.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 256 GB each). CPU model not named. The docs comparisons page gives no hardware.
corrections.caveats: baseline_in_list=false: the main comparisons are against distributed pandas-API systems (Dask DataFrame, Modin on Ray, pandas API on Spark). The paper includes pandas only on the single-node census/plasticc pipelines, where it is slowest (figure only). The paper is by the Xorbits authors, so it is first-party even though peer-reviewed. Versions are stated (Xorbits 0.6.3, pandas 2.1.1, PySpark 3.5.0, Dask 2023.9, Modin 0.24.1), with default configurations and 7 runs dropping the max and min, but no CPU model. The paper notes that TPC-H via the pandas API is 'fundamentally unfair' vs SQL systems. The last default-branch commit was 2025-04-21 (about 17 months ago), so it is stale.

notes: The comparisons-page numbers match. I upgraded C to B because the arXiv companion paper is confirmed published at ICDE 2024 (peer-reviewed industrial track). Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 1,199 stars, main last commit 2025-04-21 (repo pushed_at 2026-02-14 is from a non-default branch).
